claims.text: A court in China systematically uses a large language model to generate judicial opinions.
In the observed judicial interaction pattern, judges make initial decisions before invoking generative AI.
In the observed judicial interaction pattern, the large language model generates reasoning based on the judges' decisions.
In the observed judicial interaction pattern, judges revise the AI-generated reasoning to produce final judgments.
The three-step judge-AI interaction pattern will remain stable irrespective of AI advances because judicial accountability ultimately rests with judges rather than machines.
The judge-AI interaction process may amplify errors and biases in judicial decision-making by reinforcing judges' prior beliefs.
An experiment with real judges provides mixed evidence regarding the hypothesis that judge-AI interaction amplifies judicial errors and biases.

evidence.description: This article reports on the systematic use of a large language model by a court in China to generate judicial opinions—arguably the first instance of this in the world.
Interaction pattern outlined: 1) judges make initial decisions;
Interaction pattern outlined: 2) the large language model generates reasoning based on the judges’ decisions;
Interaction pattern outlined: 3) judges revise the reasoning generated by AI to make the final judgment.
We contend that this pattern is typical and will remain stable irrespective of advances in AI technologies, given that judicial accountability ultimately rests with judges rather than machines.

Drawing on extensive research in behavioral sciences, we propose that this interaction process between judges and AI may amplify errors and biases in judicial decision-making by reinforcing judges’ prior beliefs.
An experiment with real judges provides mixed evidence.

methodologies.name: Court Case Study and Behavioral Experiment
methodologies.description: A case study analyzing the real-world deployment of an LLM in a court in Shenzhen, China, combined with a behavioral experiment involving real judges.
conditions: Real-world court setting in Shenzhen, China

limitations.text: The experiment testing whether judge-AI interaction amplifies errors and biases produced mixed evidence rather than conclusive results.
